analysis.one_liner: Creates a national single-payer health insurance program covering every US resident, with no deductibles or copays for most care.
analysis.headline: The bill to create a universal, single-payer health insurance program was referred to five House committees in June 1992, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee coverage, CHAMPUS, and duplicative private health insurance with a single national health insurance program run by the states under federal standards. Every US resident would be enrolled automatically and issued a health card. It would cover hospital and doctor care, prescriptions, mental health, drug and alcohol treatment, and long-term care, with no deductibles or copays for acute and preventive care. It would be financed by new income-based premiums, a higher corporate tax rate, and higher payroll taxes, while hospitals would be paid from fixed annual budgets and the government would set and negotiate drug and equipment prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Every US resident would gain health coverage with no deductibles, coinsurance, or copays for acute and preventive services, and coverage that follows them between states and jobs. Families would no longer face medical bills for covered care, seniors would keep full coverage as Medicare is folded in, and people needing long-term care or mental health and addiction treatment would gain coverage they largely lacked. Low-income families would be protected from cost-sharing on those services.

how_it_helps.text: Every US citizen, national, and lawful resident alien would be entitled to health benefits under a state health insurance program, with automatic enrollment at birth or immigration and a universal health insurance card [S2] [S3].
There would be no deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments for comprehensive acute and preventive services, and providers would be barred from balance billing patients for covered services [S2] [S3].

Benefits would cover mental health services, drug and alcohol abuse treatment, and long-term care including home and community-based services, with income-related cost-sharing that cannot block families below 185 percent of the poverty line from necessary care [S2] [S3].

The bill would expand primary care in underserved areas through health center grants, an expanded National Health Service Corps, and a goal that half of medical residents train as primary care physicians [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and employers would pay new income-based national health insurance premiums; the bill also raises the top corporate income tax rate, the employer and self-employment hospital insurance tax, and imposes a surtax. Hospitals would be paid from fixed annual global budgets and would lose the ability to bill anyone but the state program for covered services. Drug and equipment makers would face government price-setting and negotiations. Private insurers would lose the market for duplicative coverage.

drawbacks.text: Financing would come from substantial new taxes: income-based premiums from individuals and employers, a higher top corporate rate, a higher hospital insurance payroll tax, and a surtax on regular and minimum taxes [S2] [S3].

The bill would abolish Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee health benefits, CHAMPUS, and duplicative private insurance as of the end of 1993, a wholesale replacement of the existing system that would force a difficult transition for tens of millions of people enrolled in those programs [S2] [S3].

Hospitals would operate under prospective global budgets and capital purchases would need state approval, a cost-control design whose critics argued could restrict timely access; the bill itself prohibits states from creating life-threatening queues and from restricting timely access through budget allocations, an acknowledgment of the risk [S2] [S3].

The government board would set prices and compile approved lists for prescription drugs, devices, and equipment and could exclude products it deemed over-priced, which manufacturers and some patients would view as restricting choice [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is enormous and concrete: universal coverage, the end of out-of-pocket costs for most care, and coverage of long-term care and mental health, paid for through progressive premiums and corporate taxes rather than deductibles and medical bills. The costs are real and large: substantial tax increases on employers and higher earners, the elimination of familiar programs like Medicare and employer plans, and a cost-control design of global budgets and price-setting whose effects on wait times and innovation were uncertain. It was a wholesale restructuring of one-sixth of the economy introduced with only three cosponsors and no committee process, so it never faced the scrutiny that would have tested its design.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 1992, referred to five House committees and then to subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers (D-MI) introduced the Health Care for Every American Act of 1992 in the House on June 25, 1992 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred jointly to five committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Post Office and Civil Service, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs [S5].

In July 1992 it was referred to subcommittees in those committees, including the Health Subcommittee, and executive comment was requested from the Department of Defense; no hearings, markups, or floor action followed [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 with the bill still pending in committee, so the bill died without any vote in either chamber [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, whose duplicative-coverage market the bill would have abolished, and pharmaceutical and device manufacturers, which would have faced government price-setting, kept the existing payment system intact. Providers were spared global budgets and mandatory assignment, and members of Congress avoided the political risk of a vote on a complete overhaul of health financing in an election year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, drug makers, and the status quo

for.what_they_did: Introduced the single-payer universal health insurance bill on June 25, 1992

for.name: 3 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it drew no Republican cosponsors

against.name: Five House committees
against.role: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Post Office and Civil Service, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs

against.name: Private health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers whose duplicate-coverage business the bill would have abolished
against.what_they_did: The industry was broadly organized against single-payer proposals in this era, as it had been against national health insurance for decades

against.role: Industries subject to government price-setting and approved-product lists under the bill
against.what_they_did: Industries facing price negotiation and price-setting have historically lobbied against such proposals

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only four House supporters, all Democrats (the sponsor and three cosponsors), and no votes ever occurred, so no partisan breakdown beyond sponsorship exists in the record.

industries.note: The bill prohibits the sale of insurance duplicating covered services and ends Medicare, Medicaid, and federal employee plans, replacing the private and public insurance system with a single state-administered program. Insurers would lose their core market; the interest runs against a universal public benefit.

A national board would determine drug prices, negotiate with manufacturers, and exclude over-priced products. Drug companies would lose pricing power; patients would gain lower drug costs, so the industry's interest runs against theirs.

Hospitals would be paid from negotiated annual global budgets, need approval for capital spending, and accept program payment as payment in full with no balance billing. They would gain guaranteed payment and an end to uncompensated care, but lose pricing freedom and budget control.

Employers would owe new premiums and taxes, but would shed responsibility for providing health benefits and deductions for employee health costs would be disallowed while national premiums became deductible. The burden shifts from a benefits-administration function to a broad tax.
The board would set prices for approved devices and equipment such as eyeglasses, hearing aids, and prosthetics and could exclude over-priced products. Manufacturers would lose pricing power.

Practitioners would be paid from prospective fee schedules with expenditure targets or by capitation or salary, with public disclosure of use patterns. They would lose billing discretion and face payment controls, but gain simple, guaranteed reimbursement and patients with no cost barriers.
